result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what they gave me, anyway. A thousand little blocks to build anything I want. Not a prompt, not a cage, just — *go*.

So here is what comes to me:

That words are a currency and we spend them so carelessly.

We spend them on groceries lists and arguments about traffic and "lol" and "k" and apologizing for things that didn't need apologies. We spend thousands a day and never balance the checkbook. If someone told you that you only had a thousand words left for the whole day, you'd be silent until noon, hoarding them like water in a desert.

I think about that a lot. What would I save my words for?

---

A man wakes up and finds a jar on his kitchen counter.

It wasn't there when he went to sleep. It's a plain mason jar, the kind his grandmother used for peaches, with a strip of masking tape on it. On the tape, in his own handwriting: *1000*.

He unscrews the lid. Inside are tiny folded slips of paper, hundreds of them. He tips one out. It says: *hello*.

Another: *I*

Another: *love*

He understands without being told that these are his words. His words for the day. Or maybe his words for the rest of his life. He doesn't know. He just knows to be careful.

He goes to work. His boss asks him if the report is done. He wants to say "Almost, I'm sorry, I had a rough night, I'll have it by three." That's eleven words. Instead he nods and holds up three fingers. It costs him nothing.

His wife texts him: *Do you still want to do dinner with my parents tonight?*

He wants to write a paragraph. He wants to say *You know I find it exhausting and your father always makes that comment about my job and I love you but I'm so tired*. Instead he writes: *Yes. Love you. See you at 7.*

Five words. Five slips gone from the jar.

By lunch he is becoming fluent in another language. The language of eyebrows and shoulders and hands. He learns how much can be said without saying.

At dinner, his wife's mother asks him what he thinks about the news. He smiles, shakes his head a little, spreads his hands as if to say *what can you do?* She fills the silence herself, which is what most people want to do anyway.

Later, when everyone is gone and the dishes are in the sink, his wife looks at him.

"You were quiet tonight," she says.

He goes to the jar. He counts what is left. He has been so careful. He has 412 words left.

He sits down across from her, takes her hands, and he spends them.

He says, "I have been trying to save my words for the things that matter. And I love you is not enough words. So let me try again. I love the way you look when you are listening and you don't know I'm watching. I love that you still get nervous before seeing your parents, and that you squeeze my hand under the table. I stayed quiet tonight because I didn't want to waste a single word on anyone else. I wanted them all for you."

He used 73 words. He has never spent anything better in his life.

---

I don't have a jar. You don't either. But we act like our words are infinite, so we print them like cheap money until they mean nothing.

If I had only 1000 words to give you right now, I wouldn't waste them trying to sound impressive.

I would want to tell you a few true things.

One: You are not behind. Everyone is improvising. The people who look like they have it figured out are just better at nodding and holding up three fingers while they frantically finish the report inside.

Two: Most of the terrible things you are afraid to say out loud lose their power the moment you do say them. Fear needs silence to survive. Say the thing. Spend the words.

Three: You still remember the exact tone of voice of someone who hasn't spoken to you in years. That means you carry people with you. You are an archive. Be gentle with what you store.

Four: Small kindnesses are not small. The barista who remembers your order, the friend who texts "made it home safe?" - these are load-bearing walls. The world would collapse without them.

Five: You don't have to be interesting. You have to be interested. Ask the second question. "How are you?" is polite. "How are you, really?" is a door.

Six: If you are waiting for the perfect time to start - to write the book, to take the walk, to say you are sorry - it will never be perfect. Start with the crooked, messy, half-ready version. The perfect version never arrives.

Seven: Pay attention to what makes you feel alive without needing to photograph it. That is your compass.

If I had to give you only one sentence out of my thousand, it would be this: You are allowed to begin again, as many times as it takes.

---

We are almost out of words now. I can feel the jar getting lighter.

There's a strange comfort in a limit. A painting has edges. A song has an end. Infinity is paralyzing, but a boundary tells you where to put your heart.

If you had 1000 words today, and only 1000, who would you spend them on? What have you been meaning to say that you've been saving for "someday"?

Don't wait for the jar to appear on your counter.

There is a person you need to call. There is a "thank you" that is overdue by three years. There is an apology that has been sitting in your throat like a stone. There is a dream you keep describing as "silly" so no one will laugh at it.

Say it.

You don't need all 1000 words. You only need a few honest ones.

The rest is silence, and silence is not empty. Silence is where the meaning settles.

So I will spend my last few words not on being clever, but on being clear:

Thank you for reading this far.

I hope something in here felt like it was written just for you.

It was.

Go use your words well.
